li.a: L'Histoire: Septembre 1792, de la rumeur au massacre (Timothy Tackett)
Sortiraparis: Ephemeris of September 2 in Paris, the September Massacres
London Review of Books: Hilary Mantel, He Roared: Danton

content.p: For five days in early September 1792, armed crowds went from prison to prison in Paris and killed the people inside. The dead included priests who had refused an oath to the new order, former royal servants and surviving Swiss Guards, but also forgers, thieves, beggars and teenagers held in a reformatory. Historians put the toll at roughly 1,100 to 1,600, about half of the city's prisoners, and the great majority of the killers were never identified.

The week still divides historians. Some read it as a spontaneous crime driven by rumour and panic, Frédéric Bluche, in 1986, argued it was premeditated by the authorities, and the philosopher Michel Foucault, as L'Histoire summarises him, described it as a legitimate act of war against internal enemies. Several of the sources below agree that the men in power in Paris, from the Commune to the Assembly to the minister of justice, did not stop it.
content.h2: A capital waiting for the Prussians
content.p: France had been at war with Austria since April 1792. By the summer Prussian and Austrian armies were advancing on France, and the Duke of Brunswick's manifesto threatened Paris with "military execution" and "complete destruction" if the royal family were harmed, in the wording Grey History quotes. After the people of Paris stormed the Tuileries Palace on 10 August and the king was imprisoned, many in the city assumed the vengeance would come.

The invaders moved fast. World History Encyclopedia dates the Prussian crossing of the border to 19 August, the fall of Longwy four days later, and the start of the siege of Verdun on 30 August. The encyclopedia calls Verdun a critical fortress: if it fell, the road to Paris would lie open through the Marne valley. The date the news reached Paris is itself uneven in the sources. Sortiraparis places the surrender on 29 August, L'Histoire says Parisians learned of it on 3 September, and Grey History says word of its imminent capitulation arrived on 2 September, with rumours that it had already fallen. Timothy Tackett's account in L'Histoire, which is the most detailed on this point, has the Commune posting the message "Aux armes! L'ennemi est à nos portes" across the city on 2 September, after Longwy's fall and the announcement of Verdun's imminent surrender.

Power in the city was split. The Legislative Assembly, the Provisional Executive Council headed by Danton, and the Insurrectionary Commune were all competing for control, Sortiraparis says. Grey History adds that a new Revolutionary Tribunal, set up on 17 August, had struck some revolutionaries as too slow.
content.h2: Arrests, searches and a rumour about the prisons
content.p: The prisons filled quickly. World History Encyclopedia says the arrests began with surviving Swiss Guards, widened to refractory priests, and then took in anyone suspected of royalist sympathies, with more than a thousand people arrested in the last two weeks of August. On the nights of 30 and 31 August armed bands carried out house-to-house visits ordered by Danton, ostensibly to collect firearms. Mantel, reviewing a biography of Danton, says the searches turned up 3,000 suspected royalists, more than the prisons could hold. Grey History cautions that the idea of grossly overcrowded prisons was partly belief, since many of those arrested during this first wave of repression were released.

Fear of what the prisoners might do mattered as much as the count. Tackett argues in L'Histoire that Paris had long traded rumours of prison breakouts, and that by spring 1792 prisons were seen as dens from which paid "brigands" might attack the Revolution. After 10 August the two fears, of plots and of the prisons, merged. The story went that once men able to fight had left for the front, royalist prisoners would break out, kill patriots and hand the city over. World History Encyclopedia quotes calls to action from the period. Marat urged good citizens to go to the Abbaye and put priests and the officers of the Swiss Guard to the sword, and the playwright Fabre d'Eglantine wrote that "the blood of traitors" should be the first offering to liberty. Marat's defenders later said he spoke in metaphor, a defence the encyclopedia finds unconvincing.

Some local bodies went further. Grey History reports that the Poissonnière section resolved that priests and other suspects in the prisons should be put to death, and that the Luxembourg section declared that prisons should be "purged by the blood of the political prisoners" before volunteers departed. On 2 September Danton gave the speech, as Mantel dates it, that ends "de l'audace, encore de l'audace, toujours de l'audace". Mantel, summarising David Lawday's biography of Danton, notes that it worked as a call for direct action among citizens as well as a strike at the external enemy.

The violence began on the afternoon of 2 September. According to World History Encyclopedia, a convoy of 24 prisoners, most of them priests in clerical dress, was being taken to the Abbaye in six cabs when a growing crowd stopped it, and 19 of the priests were hacked to death. Grey History says some federated volunteers and National Guardsmen escorting the prisoners joined the attackers rather than protecting them.

The crowd then went to the Carmes convent, which World History Encyclopedia says held 150 priests and Grey History says held as many as 200. Priests were forced into the garden and a roll was called. When a Commune official arrived, the encyclopedia says, he organised the killing rather than ending it, and a few prisoners were "acquitted". According to the same account, 115 priests died that day. Grey History says the victims included the Archbishop of Arles.

On 3 September the Abbaye was attacked again. World History Encyclopedia says roughly two-thirds of its prisoners died there, with Stanislas Maillard acting as judge and other sans-culottes as jurors. Maillard, it notes, had led the women's march on Versailles in 1789. Prisoners were brought before him one at a time, and the verdict was most often death, carried out on the spot. The encyclopedia quotes a surviving prisoner, the soldier Jourgniac de Saint-Méard, who describes the silence in which the killing went on, broken by screams, sword blows and cries of "Vive la Nation!".

The killing then reached other buildings. Sortiraparis counts nine sites in all, among them the Conciergerie, the Châtelet and the Bicêtre hospital; Tackett's list adds the Bernardins and says Bicêtre also served as a reformatory for minors. Bicêtre and the Salpêtrière held few political prisoners. World History Encyclopedia gives 162 dead at Bicêtre, 43 of them under 18 and the youngest 12, and says 40 prostitutes were killed at the Salpêtrière after being sexually assaulted. Grey History gives a lower number of 35 women for the Salpêtrière, and says about thirty juvenile detainees were killed. republique.de records that by 4 September ordinary criminals had become victims, and that the violence subsided on 5 September, with a tribunal still sitting at La Force until 6 September, when the killings ended. World History Encyclopedia ends the episode on 7 September.

The killers did not simply slaughter. Several sources describe improvised courts, with prisoners questioned briefly and sent either out of the gate to freedom or out to the waiting crowd. Tackett says prisoners held for debt, family quarrels or minor offences were often freed, as were most women, whereas counter-revolutionaries and those held for theft, forgery and murder were pushed outside and killed by volunteer executioners with swords, axes, pikes and clubs. World History Encyclopedia calls these tribunals a facade of legality. According to Grey History, news came during the Carmes killings that prisoners should be tried by improvised tribunals rather than killed indiscriminately, though from an unknown source.

The best-known victim was Marie-Thérèse, Princesse de Lamballe. She was a close friend of Marie Antoinette and had been arrested after the fall of the Tuileries. World History Encyclopedia says that on 3 September she was taken from her cell at La Force before a makeshift tribunal and asked to swear two oaths, one to liberty and equality and another denouncing the king, queen and monarchy. She agreed to the first and refused the second, and was then told she could leave. The encyclopedia explains that this was a code for execution, and quotes an eyewitness who said blows of a hammer "laid her low". It adds that accounts of what was done to her body differ, that one claim, that the crowd ate her heart, is dubious, and that it is generally agreed her head was cut off and carried on a pike toward the Temple, where the royal family was held. The same text says word of the plan reached the queen first and she fainted. Sortiraparis says the head was displayed beneath the queen's window.
content.h2: Who were the victims, and who were the killers
content.p: Many people assume the dead were mainly aristocrats and priests. The historians quoted here say otherwise. Grey History quotes a count of 223 priests and other "political" victims, no more than a quarter of the dead, with the rest common criminals, and cites the historian George Lefebvre for the view that political prisoners were a small subset. Tackett, in L'Histoire, makes the same point from the other side, calling common criminals three-quarters of the victims and asking why the Parisian elites then backed the killings or treated them as a necessary evil.

The killers are harder to count. Grey History reports that they were largely National Guardsmen, provincial volunteers and Parisian sans-culottes, and that most sources put their number at about 300 or fewer. Tackett writes that their identities will never be known, although many were probably guardsmen and volunteers who had risked their lives at the Tuileries three weeks earlier and were about to leave for the front. In his reading they probably saw the killings as both revenge and a service to the city.

The Assembly twice sent delegations to try to halt the killing, Tackett writes, and both failed, with deputies threatened by the crowd. It also issued a vague appeal for calm, but was mostly absorbed by news from the front. The Commune, in the L'Histoire glossary, did not provoke the massacres but did not try to control them. Sortiraparis is blunter, saying that neither authorities, National Guard, government, Assembly nor Commune opposed the killings. Danton was the justice minister. Mantel says he did nothing to stop them, and quotes him as saying that no power on earth could have stopped the national vengeance. republique.de says Marat later told the National Convention that the people had followed his call, a statement that caused outrage.

Tackett found that none of the Paris newspapers of the time condemned the killings, whether radical or moderate. Private letters reflected the same acceptance. One writer called the people to be pitied, not blamed, and a Saint-Sulpice resident noted in his diary that it was better to kill the devil before he kills you. There were exceptions: the bookseller Nicolas Ruault, who had tried to save a neighbour held at the Abbaye, wrote to his brother on 8 September of shame and crime. Shock set in only in the following weeks and months, Tackett says, as the rumours faded.

The French victory at Valmy on 20 September eased the panic, World History Encyclopedia notes. In the aftermath, the encyclopedia says, each revolutionary faction blamed the others for the massacres, though none had stopped them. Grey History says the affair dominated the first months of the Convention, sharpened the quarrel between Girondins and Montagnards, and weakened the Girondins' ties with the Paris sans-culottes. News of the killings, World History Encyclopedia says, turned opinion across Europe against the Revolution and set off a new wave of emigration, this time including middle-class families. Both it and Grey History, along with Sortiraparis, describe the week as a step toward the Terror, because it made violence an accepted political tool.
